extracted.subtask_description: Reporting and compiling wartime dispatches and related human-interest and political items for a newspaper audience, synthesizing official communiques, correspondent dispatches, eyewitnesses and agency reports into news copy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source attribution (official communiques and monitors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Statements and claims are attributed to named sources such as official communiques, bulletins, monitors and foreign newspapers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples in text: “the midnight communique said”, “the midnight Moscow bulletin, recorded by the Soviet monitor”, “Moscow disclosed last night”, “Reports from Stockholm said”, “recorded by U. S. government monitors”. Always identify the originating source for military or political claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantified casualty and equipment reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide specific numeric counts for casualties and materiel losses (men, tanks, planes) when reporting battles and attacks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: “Germans had lost 4,500 more men and 95 tanks”, “Almost 17,000 Germans have been killed in this area in the last three days”, “Twenty-nine planes were destroyed on the ground”. Include precise figures as reported and attribute them to sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographic specificity and distance measurements
rubrics_metrics.description: Give precise locations and distances (miles inside borders, miles from cities, rail junctions) to situate advances and retreats.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: “50-mile gain”, “Olshana, 18 miles north”, “ten miles inside Estonia”, “within fifty miles of the Russian-German 1939 boundary”, “Only 85 miles to the southwest of Lutsk lies Lwow”. Use rail junctions and city names to orient readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Description of military maneuvers and tactical outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe the nature of operations (encirclement, outflanking maneuvers, tightening rings, aerial blockades) and the immediate tactical results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: “encircling lines around ten Nazi divisions”, “well-executed, outflanking maneuver”, “tightening ring of Red army forces”, “The Soviet air force clamped an aerial blockade over the area”. Explain operational effect (surrender, destruction, attempted breakouts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion of official orders and ceremonial announcements
rubrics_metrics.description: Report official orders, proclamations and ceremonial acts issued by leaders as newsworthy elements tied to military events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: “Stalin’s ‘special order of the day to Gen. Nikolai Vatutin’”, “Stalin Orders Salute”, “ordered twenty artillery salvos (to be fired from 224 guns)”. Quote or summarize the order and note associated ceremonial responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextualization and skepticism about propaganda or rumors
rubrics_metrics.description: Flag and contextualize propaganda, opposing narratives, and rumors; advise readers when reports may be Axis/Allied-inspired misinformation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: “The British Ambassador also denounced what he called ‘fantastic rumors’ ... Pay no attention to rumors of this kind”, “Gerirermprese-has begun to use what it described as the imminence of an Allied invasion ... to explain continued reverses”. Note source and suggest caution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humanitarian and evacuation reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Include information on civilian movements, refugee flows, evacuations, mobilizations and relief preparations related to military operations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: “Frightened citizens were reported swarming aboard a few ships in the harbor of Riga”, “approximately 1,500,000 residents ... were moving on Germany”, “the Nazi-dominated regime in Lithuania mobilized new classes”. Provide scale, routes and destination details when available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical background and parallels
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide historical context or parallels that illuminate the significance of current operations (e.g., past battles, prior occupations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: “treading on historic soil where Russian blood flowed in the first World war”, “the Czar’s armies suffered 1,000,000 casualties in their 1916 offensive”. Use past events to frame current gains or losses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Datelines and agency bylines to situate dispatches
rubrics_metrics.description: Use datelines and agency attributions (e.g., MOSCOW, Feb. 5 (A.P.)) to show where and by whom reports originate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: “MOSCOW, Feb. 5 (A. P.)—”, “Anzio, Italy, Feb. 5 (A. P.).—”. Place these at the start of dispatches to indicate provenance and timeliness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of firsthand interviews and exclusive correspondent material
rubrics_metrics.description: Include interviews, exclusive remarks and eyewitness anecdotes from named individuals to add human interest and detail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: “told me in an exclusive interview today”, Prince Stefano Borghese’s recollections about Edda and Ciano. Attribute quotes and personal anecdotes to identified speakers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reconstruction and economic-statistics reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: When covering post-combat recovery, give concrete reconstruction statistics (money allocated, livestock, seed tonnage, factories) to illustrate scale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: “The government has allotted 16,000,000,000 rubles ... the principal provinces ... aided have been ...”, “1,723,201 cows, chickens and 96,324 tons of seed”. Use exact figures and describe sources of supplies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naming individuals and awarding details in honors coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: List decorated personnel with ranks, hometowns and the specific honors and citation summaries when reporting military awards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: long lists of names with awards such as Silver Star, Distinguished Flying Cross, Air Medal; citations describing gallantry. Include rank and location for each person.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multi-theater breadth in a single news compilation
rubrics_metrics.description: Cover developments across multiple fronts and theaters (Eastern Front, Baltic, Pacific, Burma, Italy, Spain, Argentina) within the same news roundup.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This article mixes dispatches from Ukraine, Estonia, New Guinea, Burma, Italy and South America; organize clearly by dateline and theater so readers can follow distinct campaigns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting enemy broadcasts and foreign-language dispatches with source verification
rubrics_metrics.description: When using enemy or foreign broadcasts (Domei, German press), report their content but indicate monitoring and translation sources and any caveats.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: “The Japanese Domei Agency ... in an English language wireless dispatch to North America”, “recorded by U. S. government monitors”. Note that such material may be propaganda and identify the monitoring body.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge information limits and uncertainty
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicitly state gaps in knowledge or when no confirmation is available rather than presenting unverified claims as fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: “there was no information yet as to whether the railway and highway ... had been cut”, “it appeared likely that the only result would be the sacrifice of thousands of lives”. Use qualifying language where reporting is incomplete.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concise, headline-focused summation
rubrics_metrics.description: Lead with a strong headline or lede that summarizes the key action or development succinctly for quick reader comprehension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example headline forms in text: “NAZIS TRY VAN TO BREAK RED TRAP” and subheads like “4,500 Germans Slain, 95 Tanks Smashed as Ukraine Encirclement Tightens.” Use pithy summaries and prominent figures in headlines.
